rounds.proof_sketch: With block_size=256, warp_id∈[0,7]. Original: warp 0 computes sum(warp_sums[0..7]) and writes to warp_sums[0]. Mutant: warps 1-7 each compute the same sum(warp_sums[0..7]) and all write the same value to warp_sums[0]. Both produce identical warp_sums[0] after the barrier.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes which warps execute the final reduction, but not the computed result. After the first __syncthreads(), warp_sums[0..7] contain fixed partial sums. In the mutant, all of warps 1-7 read these same values, compute the identical total, and write the same result to warp_sums[0]. The race condition is benign since all writes are identical. After the second __syncthreads(), warp_sums[0] contains the correct total regardless of which implementation runs. This structural equivalence holds for ALL possible input values.
rounds.kill_strategy: This mutant is unkillable under the fixed configuration. The equivalence is structural—the code paths produce identical results for ANY input values. The only way to expose a difference would be if block_size < 32 (single warp), which would cause the mutant to skip the reduction entirely. However, block_size=256 is fixed in the contract.
rounds.recommendations: When testing relational operator mutations on warp-level code, verify whether the mutation affects WHICH threads execute versus WHAT they compute. Mutations that only change task distribution among warps (all computing the same result) are structurally equivalent. Consider adding assertions that verify reduction participation counts, not just final values.
